learningObjectives.title: Rural change and the rural-urban continuum
The rural-urban continuum and settlement links

questions.q: What does the term 'urbanisation' mean?
options: An increase in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas
The movement of people from towns to the countryside
The spreading of a city outwards into surrounding villages
The decline of industry within an inner-city area
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a population living in towns and cities rather than rural areas.

questions.q: What is 'counterurbanisation'?
options: The movement of people out of large cities into rural areas and smaller settlements
The rapid growth of shanty towns on the edge of cities
The building of new high-rise flats in city centres
The migration of people from rural areas into cities for work
questions.explain: Counterurbanisation is the outward movement of people from major urban areas to rural or smaller settlements.

questions.q: A city is usually classed as a 'megacity' once its population reaches at least:
options: 10 million
1 million
5 million
50 million
questions.explain: A megacity is generally defined as an urban area with a population of 10 million or more.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why rapid urbanisation occurs in many lower-income countries?
options: Rural-urban migration combined with high natural increase in cities
People moving from cities to retire in the countryside
A fall in the total national population
The conversion of farmland into national parks
questions.explain: Rapid urbanisation is driven by people migrating from rural to urban areas alongside high birth rates within the cities.

questions.q: What is 'suburbanisation'?
options: The outward growth of a town or city into the surrounding rural-urban fringe
The rebuilding of run-down inner-city housing
The loss of population from remote rural villages
The concentration of shops in a central business district
questions.explain: Suburbanisation is the outward spread of an urban area, developing housing and estates on its edges.

questions.q: The zone where the built-up edge of a town meets the surrounding countryside is called the:
options: Rural-urban fringe
Central business district
Inner city
Green belt core
questions.explain: The rural-urban fringe is the transition zone where urban land uses meet rural land uses at a settlement's edge.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a 'green belt'?
options: To restrict the outward sprawl of built-up areas and protect countryside
To provide low-cost housing for city workers
To attract new factories to the edge of cities
To increase the density of city-centre development
questions.explain: A green belt is a ring of protected open land around a city that limits urban sprawl.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'push' factor encouraging people to leave rural areas?
options: Lack of jobs and poor services in the countryside
Better healthcare available in the city
Higher wages offered in urban factories
Wider range of entertainment in towns
questions.explain: Push factors are negatives about the origin area, such as limited rural employment and services.

questions.q: Which of the following is a 'pull' factor attracting migrants to cities?
options: The prospect of better-paid employment
Drought damaging local crops
A shortage of schools in the village
Flooding of farmland
questions.explain: Pull factors are positives about the destination, such as the promise of higher-paid urban jobs.

questions.q: A village where most residents travel to work in a nearby city is often described as a:
options: Commuter (dormitory) village
Honeypot village
Shanty settlement
Conurbation
questions.explain: A commuter or dormitory village is one whose residents mainly work elsewhere and return home to sleep.

questions.q: Which is a likely social effect of counterurbanisation on a small rural village?
options: Rising house prices that can price out local younger people
A rapid fall in the total number of houses
The complete loss of all road links to the city
A large increase in heavy manufacturing industry
questions.explain: Newcomers with higher incomes push up house prices, making it harder for local young people to afford homes.

questions.q: What is 'rural depopulation'?
options: A decline in the population of remote or isolated rural areas
An increase in tourists visiting the countryside
The building of new estates in the countryside
The growth of farming employment in villages
questions.explain: Rural depopulation is the loss of people from rural areas, often as younger residents move away.

questions.q: What does 're-urbanisation' describe?
options: The movement of people back into city centres, often after regeneration
The abandonment of city centres for the countryside
The first growth of cities during the Industrial Revolution
The spread of farming into the rural-urban fringe
questions.explain: Re-urbanisation is the return of population to inner urban areas, frequently following regeneration schemes.

questions.q: How can a high number of second homes affect a rural community?
options: It can reduce demand for local services as many houses stand empty for much of the year
It guarantees more full-time jobs in local shops all year round
It always lowers house prices for local residents
It increases the number of school-age children in the village
questions.explain: Second homes left empty for much of the year cut year-round demand, threatening shops, schools and services.

questions.q: A former farming village near a motorway junction has gained several new housing estates, and most residents now drive to jobs in the nearby city. This village is best described as having undergone:
options: Suburbanisation into a commuter village
Rural depopulation
Deindustrialisation
Re-urbanisation
questions.explain: New estates and residents commuting to the city show suburban growth turning the village into a commuter settlement.

questions.q: In a remote village, the bus service is cut, the shop closes and the primary school shuts. Which process does this sequence best illustrate?
options: A cycle of rural decline linked to depopulation
Counterurbanisation raising house prices
Rapid re-urbanisation of the countryside
The growth of a honeypot site
questions.explain: Falling population reduces demand, closing services, which in turn encourages more people to leave in a downward spiral.

questions.q: What is meant by 'urban regeneration'?
options: Improving and redeveloping run-down or derelict parts of a city
Moving industry out of cities into rural areas
Extending the green belt around a city
Increasing rural-urban migration into a city
questions.explain: Urban regeneration involves investing in and rebuilding declining urban areas to improve them.

questions.q: In Country X, 30% of people lived in urban areas in 1990 and 65% did so in 2020. What does this change show?
options: Rapid urbanisation over the period
Counterurbanisation over the period
A fall in the total population
A move towards a more rural society
questions.explain: A rising percentage of people living in urban areas indicates urbanisation is taking place quickly.

questions.q: The 'rural-urban continuum' is best described as:
options: A gradual change in settlement character from remote rural to dense urban areas
A sharp boundary line separating towns from villages
A government policy protecting farmland
The daily journey made by commuters to work
questions.explain: The rural-urban continuum recognises that settlements grade gradually from deeply rural to fully urban rather than fitting neat categories.

questions.q: In a rural area, a 'honeypot site' is a place that:
options: Attracts large numbers of visitors and tourists
Has lost most of its population
Is protected from all development
Contains only second homes
questions.explain: A honeypot site is an attractive location that draws in many tourists, which can put pressure on the local area.
